title: How Dying Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how dying works, starting with population estimates (about 107 billion people have ever lived, per Carl Haub of the Population Reference Bureau) and the shifting definition of death from the soul leaving the body to brain death (Harvard 1968 higher-brain definition versus the Uniform Determination of Death Act's whole-brain standard). They cover historical death checks, the link between organ transplantation and brain-death criteria, what different deaths feel like (drowning, heart attack, bleeding out, electrocution, falling, hanging, burning, natural causes), and the preactive and active phases of dying (cyanosis, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, death rattle, hearing lasting longest, palliative and hospice care). They then discuss post-mortem changes (pupil dilation, lacrimal mortis, tache noire, algor, rigor and livor mortis, putrefaction, purge fluid, coffin birth, de-gloving), physician-assisted suicide and the Freud and Hunter Thompson cases, and the top five regrets of the dying. The episode ends with a listener mail about spider-eye flashlight tricks.

segments.title: Opening banter and population of humanity
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, then Josh cites Carl Haub's Population Reference Bureau estimate that about 107 billion people have ever lived, all of whom share death.
topics: how many people have ever lived

segments.title: Ernest Becker and the denial of death
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the psychologist Ernest Becker and his book The Denial of Death, and note Molly Edmonds' article on the definition of death.

segments.title: Historical death checks and medical technology
segments.summary: They discuss how death was once declared by priests using feathers and mirrors, how stethoscopes and later needle-and-flag tests changed checks, and how life support has complicated the definition of death.

segments.title: Brain death and the definition of death
segments.summary: They cover the French coma depasse concept, the 1968 Harvard definition of irreversible coma, the presidential commission's Uniform Determination of Death Act favoring whole-brain death over higher-brain death, and the link to organ transplantation in the 1960s.

segments.title: Three types of death and what dying feels like
segments.summary: The hosts divide deaths into accidental, violent, and natural, then discuss the experience of drowning, heart attack, blood loss, electrocution, falling (including Golden Gate Bridge jumpers), and hanging.

segments.title: Burning, smoke inhalation, and natural death
segments.summary: They discuss burning and smoke inhalation, then natural death from chronic disease in the US, with heart disease and cancer as leading causes, and the rise of frailty as a form of old-age death.

segments.title: Preactive and active phases of dying
segments.summary: They describe the preactive phase (sleepiness, cyanosis, mottling, withdrawal, settling unfinished business) and the active phase (confusion, hallucinations of the dead, irregular breathing, loss of senses with hearing lasting longest), and advise families on how to behave.

segments.title: Death rattle, agonal phase, and palliative care
segments.summary: They explain the death rattle and agonal phase as signs of roughly forty-eight hours left, plus other active-dying changes such as blood pressure drop, spasms, and cold extremities, and discuss palliative care and hospice workers.

segments.title: Immediate postmortem signs: pupils, tears, eyes
segments.summary: After death the pupils dilate, and lacrimal mortis (a final tear) is described from a New Zealand study. They discuss closing eyes after death and tache noire, the dark strip over an open eye.

segments.title: Decomposition: algor, rigor, livor mortis, and putrefaction
segments.summary: They run through algor mortis, rigor mortis, livor mortis, then putrefaction: gut microbes, color changes, bloating, purge fluid, coffin birth, hair and nail changes, and de-gloving from airbags.

segments.title: Physician-assisted suicide and famous deaths
segments.summary: They discuss end-of-life choice, advance directives and living wills, ICU deaths, the case for physician-assisted suicide, and examples of Hunter S. Thompson's death and Sigmund Freud's physician-assisted death.

segments.title: Top five regrets of the dying
segments.summary: Chuck reads the five most common regrets identified by a hospice nurse, including living true to oneself, working less, expressing feelings, staying in touch with friends, and allowing oneself to be happier.

segments.title: Listener mail: spider flashlight trick and shout-out
segments.summary: A listener from Thousand Oaks, California, thanks the hosts for the flashlight trick for spotting spiders and asks for a shout-out to her fiance Danny before their wedding.
